cells.tense: You're at the table with this now, steering it, and the steering is yours.
cells.ask: Say out loud one thing you're growing and the reason it matters to you — one sentence, once.
cells.core:
You're deciding what gets held and what gets let go, and you're doing it without force. Care and direction are running together here — you grow what's yours and you also say when something is finished. That combination is rarer than either half, and it's what lets what you've grown stand on its own.

The weight in this is that you're the one who has to call it done. Tending that won't finish anything turns into holding on, and you feel that pull. Saying why you tend it — the reason underneath — is what keeps your hand open when the moment to release comes.
cells.sheetLine: You hold care and direction together, and both are chosen.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, chosen care
cells.place: the place where direction gets chosen

cells.tense: You're living in the version where it's already handled, already finished, already grown — and pulling today toward that picture.
cells.ask: Write one sentence about what growing this looks like today — no plans, no outcome, just today's shape.
cells.core:
You're racing to look after things that aren't yet yours to look after, and doing it ahead of time. The picture of how it should all turn out has gotten so vivid that today's version feels like a failure next to it. You're not tending the thing in front of you — you're rehearsing the ending before the middle has happened.

A garden gets tended at the pace it grows, not at the pace you can picture it finished. When the finished picture is that clear, it's tempting to skip the slow middle — but the middle is where the work actually happens. One true sentence about today shrinks the picture back to size and puts your hand on the actual soil.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering toward the finished picture and skipping the growing.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, chosen care
cells.place: the place where direction gets chosen

cells.tense: You set this down a while back, and you're still standing where you left it.
cells.ask: Put one hour in your calendar this week for one small thing you've been growing, and give it that hour.
cells.core:
You know how to look after something — you've done it before — and right now nothing of your own is getting that from you. The direction you used to set, you let it go quiet, and the quiet has started to feel like the shape of things rather than a season. What's gone is picking it back up, not the ability.

Care that doesn't exhaust starts with something small enough to finish. An hour on one real thing brings the muscle back — not because the hour fixes anything, but because setting a direction is a thing you do, and doing it once starts it up again. This doesn't refill by thinking about it; it refills by being used on something that fits.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped growing anything of your own, and picking one thing back up is what's missing.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, chosen care
cells.place: the place where direction gets chosen

cells.tense: You're already steering this, and you're talking about it like it's just how things are.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you did this week that was a choice about direction — not a task, not a job — and read it back to yourself.
cells.core:
The deciding is happening — what gets attention, what gets held, what gets let go — every week. It just doesn't feel like deciding from the inside; it feels like the shape of the work, the demands of the situation, what any reasonable person would do. Somewhere along the way it stopped being credited to you.

A person tending something is also the one who decides which things are theirs to tend. Writing one decision down puts your name back on it. Not to take credit — to remember that this wasn't just happening to you; you were in it, choosing, the whole time.
cells.sheetLine: You're choosing direction. You've been calling it just how things work.

attempts.check: The draft risks saying the person is caring for something in particular — a garden, a team, a person — which the record never establishes; the card gives a way of tending, not an object, so the cells keep a placeholder ('what's yours to tend', 'the thing you're growing') rather than naming it. A reader might reasonably say they don't feel balanced at all, or that nothing is growing in their life right now; the asks survive that because each one is a physical act done today about how choices get made, not a claim about how they feel. The line that would serve the writer more than the reader is any sentence about 'stewardship' as a noble posture — cut; the sheetLine in Balanced ('You hold care and direction together...') is the only sentence kept close to the spine because the person needs something to stand on, and it is narrowed to a capacity, not their biography.
